newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: South Korea hit by financial crisis after strikes.
newsitem.headline: South Korea hit by financial crisis after strikes.

text.p: South Korean President Kim Young-sam on Monday ordered a probe into the troubled Hanbo Group amid opposition accusations of government misconduct in an unfolding loan scandal.
Kim's son lashed out at rumours linking him to one of the most serious crises in the country's corporate history.
Hanbo Steel, which defaulted on debts last week, borrowed five trillion won ($5.8 billion), about 20 times its net worth, mainly to fund a huge expansion project.

The opposition called the loans South Korea's biggest financial scandal and seized on the issue to attack Kim, already on the defensive during a presidential election year after a botched effort to reform labour laws.
"President Kim ordered a thorough probe into the Hanbo case to determine how the project had been financed so as not to leave a speck of suspicion," a presidential Blue House spokesman said.

"I can swear with confidence that neither President Kim, his family members nor those in his inner circle have anything to do with the Hanbo case," newspapers quoted Kim's chief political secretary as saying.
A prosecution task force began reviewing the financial records of Hanbo Steel, flagship of South Korea's 14th largest industrial conglomerate.
The main opposition National Congress for New Politics and the United Liberal Democratic Party demanded a parliamentary probe into how so much money was funnelled into a shaky company.
"The Hanbo incident is the biggest ever power-linked financial irregularity," their statement said. The collapse had "dealt a fatal shock" to the economy.
Banks could not have given "unlimited financial support to Hanbo Group unless there was protection and influence peddling at the heart of the power, including the Blue House", the statement said.
Kim Hyun-chol, President Kim's second son, threatened legal action to defend his reputation.

"I don't understand why I'm mentioned in Hanbo-related rumours," he said in an interview with the Joong-Ang Ilbo daily. "If someone names my name in a claim of complicity, I will formally take legal steps."
The ruling New Korea Party agreed to the investigation on condition it did not hamper a separate probe by state prosecutors, a party statement said.
It accused the opposition of "serving as a loudhailer to spread unfounded, irresponsible rumours" in the run-up to presidential elections in December.
"Our party believes there must not be a sanctuary from the investigation, whether a person belongs to the ruling camp or opposition," it said. "We will tackle this matter with determination."
The constitution bars Kim from seeking a second term, but he is believed to want to install a protege in office.
His popularity, already ebbing, was further battered when the forced passage of a new labour law last month sparked some of the worst strikes in South Korean history.
In a humiliating retreat, Kim agreed to send the bill back to parliament for debate.

The Hanbo crisis triggered alarm in South Korean financial markets. There was concern over its impact on sagging bank profits and the prospect it could force up interest rates and lead to a credit crunch.
The central bank pumped a further two trillion won into the banking system to prevent a credit squeeze after injecting one trillion won last Friday.
Last week Moody's Investor Service placed under review for possible downgrade ratings of Korea Exchange Bank, Korea First Bank, and Cho Hung Bank, which have the biggest exposure to Hanbo.
Nervous investors dumped shares, sending the main index down by 2.98 percent to 664.70.
